title: Model Selection and Cost Optimization
description: Learn how to choose the right model for each task and control costs without sacrificing quality or safety.

data.text: Most teams overpay for AI by using one expensive model for every request. A better strategy is model routing: choose model size and capability based on task risk, complexity, and required quality. This lesson gives you a practical system for that.
Why model routing matters

AI model pricing varies by orders of magnitude. A frontier model like GPT-6 Astra or Claude Fable 5.1 can cost around 100x more per token than a small, fast model like GPT-6 Luna or Claude Haiku 5.5. For individual users, this difference is often negligible. For teams running thousands of AI calls per day — in customer support pipelines, content workflows, or automated analysis — it translates directly to budget.

The insight behind model routing is that not all tasks require frontier-level intelligence. Classifying a support ticket, translating a short sentence, or extracting a date from a document is a fundamentally different problem than writing a 2,000-word technical report or reasoning through a complex legal scenario. Using a powerful model for the former is like hiring a senior consultant to sort your mail.

data.text: Understanding model tiers

Every major AI provider now offers a tiered model family — small, medium, and large variants of the same underlying architecture. Smaller models are faster and cheaper; larger models are more capable at complex reasoning but slower and more expensive. The names vary by provider but the pattern is consistent.

data.title: Model families change faster than the tier structure
data.text: Specific model names and prices change with every release cycle. What stays stable is the tier structure: every provider offers small, mid, and large variants. Design your routing policy around tiers, not specific model names, and update the specific model references quarterly.

data.text: Classifying task risk

Risk level is the most important axis for routing decisions. A mistake in a low-risk task (e.g., internal brainstorming) costs nothing. A mistake in a high-risk task (e.g., a client-facing legal summary) can have real consequences. Three factors drive risk: the consequence of an error, whether a human will review the output before it is acted on, and whether the output is reversible.

rows: Internal use only; human will review; mistakes are easily corrected

Published or acted on with minimal review; mistakes have financial, legal, or reputational consequences

data.title: Human review is not optional for high-risk outputs
data.text: Even the best frontier models make mistakes. For any output that will be used to make a financial decision, published under your brand, or relied on for safety-critical guidance — a human must review it before it goes out. Model tier selection reduces the probability of error; it does not eliminate it.
Cost optimization tactics

data.title: High-impact cost levers
items: Shorten prompts: remove repeated context and unnecessary verbosity
Constrain output length when full detail is not needed
Cache repeated prompts and standard responses
Use two-stage workflows: cheap first pass, expensive final pass only when needed
Track cost per workflow, not just cost per request

data.text: Prompt efficiency: the most overlooked cost driver

AI APIs charge by the token — both for input (your prompt) and output (the model's reply). Bloated system prompts, redundant context, and unconstrained output length are the most common sources of avoidable cost. A system prompt that repeats the same instruction five times in slightly different words is not more effective than stating it once clearly — it is just more expensive.

rows: Pasting the full company background into every prompt
Use a short identifier and store context server-side; inject only what is relevant
"Summarize this document" with no length guidance
"Summarize in 3 bullet points, max 20 words each"
Distil to a 100-word instruction set; test that quality holds
Sending 40 prior turns for every new request
Summarize older turns; only send the last 5–10 turns verbatim
Sending a full 10,000-row CSV to the model
Pre-filter or aggregate data before sending; models do not need all rows to spot a trend

data.text: Caching: paying once for repeated prompts

Prompt caching allows the API to reuse the computed representation of a prompt prefix that has already been processed. If your system prompt or a large document is sent identically at the start of every request, caching can reduce the cost of that prefix by 50–90% depending on the provider. Anthropic's Claude API and OpenAI's API both support prompt caching. For high-volume pipelines with stable system prompts, enabling caching is often the single highest-ROI optimization available.

data.caption: How prompt caching works — the cached prefix is computed once and reused across requests
data.definition:
sequenceDiagram

  participant API as Model API

  App->>API: Request 1: [System prompt (1000 tokens)] + [User message]
  API->>Cache: Compute and store system prompt prefix

  App->>API: Request 2: [Same system prompt] + [Different user message]
  API->>Cache: Check cache — hit!
  Cache-->>API: Return cached prefix
  API-->>App: Response (prefix cost reduced 50–90%)

data.text: Two-stage workflows: cheap filter, expensive finisher

A two-stage workflow uses a small, cheap model to classify or pre-process a request, and only escalates to a larger model when the task genuinely requires it. This pattern is extremely common in production AI systems.

data.caption: Two-stage routing: a small model filters requests before an expensive model is invoked

data.text: Example: a customer support pipeline receives 500 messages per day. A small model classifies each message into one of three categories — simple FAQ, product issue, or billing dispute. FAQ answers are generated by the small model directly. Product and billing issues are routed to a larger model with access to the customer's account history. The result: 70% of requests are resolved cheaply, and the expensive model is invoked only where its quality genuinely matters.
Latency: the other optimization axis

Cost is only one dimension. Latency — how long the model takes to respond — matters for any user-facing application. A frontier model producing an excellent answer in 15 seconds is a poor choice for a real-time chat interface. A small model answering in under a second is often the right call, even if quality is slightly lower.

Mid-tier model is usually the right balance

data.title: Use streaming for better perceived latency
data.text: All major model APIs support streaming — returning response tokens as they are generated rather than waiting for the full response to complete. For user-facing applications, streaming makes a 10-second frontier model feel far more responsive. The user sees text appearing immediately rather than waiting for a loading spinner to resolve.
Measuring quality to validate routing decisions

Routing decisions should be validated with data, not just intuition. The risk of over-optimizing for cost is that quality degrades in ways that are invisible until a customer complains or an error surfaces in production. Build measurement into your pipeline from the start.

data.title: Practical ways to measure output quality:
items: Human spot-check: sample 5–10% of outputs per week; rate them on a simple 1–5 scale for accuracy and usefulness.
LLM-as-judge: use a separate model call to rate the quality of outputs from your pipeline. Prompt it with a rubric and a sample output and ask for a structured score.
Task-specific metrics: for classification tasks, measure accuracy against a labelled test set; for code, measure test pass rate; for summarization, measure coverage of key facts.
Downstream outcome tracking: if your AI output feeds a human decision, track the decision error rate over time as a proxy for upstream quality.
Regression testing: keep a golden set of test cases and run them against every new model version to detect quality regressions before they reach production.

data.text: Building a routing matrix for your team

A routing matrix is a simple internal document that maps your team's recurring AI tasks to a default model tier, a quality threshold, and an escalation rule. It does not need to be automated — even a shared spreadsheet used by a team of five can reduce AI spend by 30–50% by preventing reflexive use of the most expensive model.

data.text: Common routing mistakes to avoid

data.title: Pitfalls that erode cost savings or quality:
items: Routing by task name rather than task risk — 'email drafting' sounds simple but a client proposal email is high-risk; a quick internal scheduling message is low-risk. Route by consequence, not category name.
Assuming cheap models cannot handle the job without testing — small models have improved dramatically. Always benchmark before assuming a task requires a frontier model.

Never revisiting routing decisions — models improve every few months. A task that required a frontier model in 2023 may be handled excellently by a small model today. Review your routing matrix quarterly.
Optimizing cost without measuring quality — cutting costs 40% while degrading quality 20% is a net loss if quality drives customer retention or trust.
Ignoring total workflow cost — a two-model routing pipeline has orchestration overhead. For very low-volume tasks, the complexity cost may outweigh the savings.

Using frontier models for output verification — using an expensive model to check the output of another expensive model doubles cost with limited upside. Use a mid-tier model or a rule-based check for verification.

data.title: Build your model routing policy
data.description: Create a simple internal routing matrix for your top 10 AI tasks.
steps: List your top 10 recurring AI tasks.
Assign each task a risk level (low/medium/high).
Set a default model tier per task.
Define escalation criteria when output quality is low.
Run for one week and compare cost and quality outcomes.
data.expectedOutcome: A repeatable routing policy that reduces spend while maintaining quality.

data.title: Model selection and cost optimization — key principles
points: Route by task risk, not habit — most tasks do not need a frontier model
Small models are much better than they were a year ago; always benchmark before assuming a task needs the largest model
Shorten prompts, constrain output length, and enable caching — these are the three highest-ROI prompt optimizations
Two-stage workflows (cheap classifier + expensive finisher) are the most effective architectural cost lever
Latency matters as much as cost for user-facing applications — use streaming for better perceived performance
Measure quality continuously; cost optimization without quality measurement is just degradation on a budget
Review your routing matrix quarterly — model capabilities change faster than most policies do
